title: HOW FAR IS “TOO FAR” BEFORE MARRIAGE? THE QUESTION CHRISTIANS KEEP ASKING—AND THE TRUTH MANY ARE AFRAID TO HEAR
paragraphs: HOW FAR IS “TOO FAR” BEFORE MARRIAGE? THE QUESTION CHRISTIANS KEEP ASKING—AND THE TRUTH MANY ARE AFRAID TO HEAR

You can save yourself for marriage and still surrender your heart to lust. You can cross boundaries you swore you would never cross and still find forgiveness in Jesus. But there is a question far more important than “How much can we do without sinning?” And the answer might change the way you love forever.
There is a moment nobody posts about.

The lights are low. The conversation has gotten quieter. You're sitting beside someone you genuinely love. Their hand finds yours. One kiss becomes another. You tell yourself you're not doing anything wrong.
You're both Christians.
You pray together.
You talk about marriage.
You even believe God brought you into each other's lives.
But somewhere between that first kiss and the moment you realize how difficult it has become to stop, something changes.
Your conscience begins whispering.
Should we be doing this?
You ignore it for a moment.
Because you love this person.
Because you intend to marry them.
Because everybody seems to be doing far more than you are.
And because, deep down, you want someone to tell you that what you're doing is still acceptable to God.
Then comes the question that has troubled countless Christian couples:
How far is too far physically before marriage?
Is kissing wrong?
What about passionate kissing?
What about lying together, touching intimately, or sleeping in the same bed without having intercourse?
What if you've already gone further?
What if you genuinely love each other?
What if you're engaged?
And what if you already crossed a line you cannot uncross?
Stay with me.
Because this is not going to be another message that simply tells you to behave yourself, makes you feel dirty, and leaves you alone with your guilt.
We're going to open Scripture.
We're going to distinguish what God actually says from what Christians sometimes assume He says.
We're going to talk about desire, self-control, temptation, shame, holiness, and the kind of love that doesn't demand access to someone's body as proof of commitment.
And before we're finished, I want you to understand something that may be especially important if you've already fallen.
Jesus did not shed His blood merely to make you feel ashamed of your past. He came to redeem you from sin and teach you how to walk in freedom.
But to understand that freedom, we have to confront something uncomfortable.
Sometimes the real danger isn't how close two people have come to having sex.
It's how comfortable they've become negotiating with temptation.
Think about that.

A couple can spend hours debating whether a certain kind of kissing is technically sinful while never asking why they're deliberately creating situations where obedience becomes increasingly difficult.
They can establish a rule that says, “We'll stop before intercourse,” while repeatedly engaging in physical intimacy that leaves both of them struggling to stop.
They can pray together on Sunday and privately compromise on Friday.
And slowly, almost imperceptibly, the question changes.
Instead of asking, “How can we honor Jesus in this relationship?”
They begin asking, “How much can we enjoy without God calling it sin?”
That's where the spiritual danger begins.
Not because physical attraction is evil.
Not because affection is automatically sinful.
And certainly not because the human body is dirty.
God created the body.
God created marriage.
God created the capacity for sexual desire.
Genesis 1:31 tells us that God saw everything He had made, and it was very good.
Genesis 2:24 describes a man and his wife becoming one flesh.
The Hebrew expression is בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad, meaning “one flesh.”
This is not merely a poetic description of physical pleasure. Within the biblical account, it describes the profound union of husband and wife, a union Jesus Himself later affirms in Matthew 19:4–6.
Sexual intimacy was never designed to be meaningless.
It belongs within a covenant where two people give themselves to one another in a faithful marital union.
That matters because the world often teaches us to separate physical intimacy from lifelong responsibility.
It tells us that if two people consent, feel strongly about each other, and intend no harm, then there is no deeper moral question to consider.
But Scripture asks us to think beyond immediate desire.
It asks what our actions mean.
What they cultivate.
What they promise.
And whether they honor the God who made us.
Listen carefully to Paul's words in 1 Thessalonians 4:3–5, from the King James Version:

“For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication: That every one of you should know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour; Not in the lust of concupiscence, even as the Gentiles which know not God.”
The Greek word translated “fornication” is πορνεία — porneia.
It is a broad term for sexual immorality. In the biblical context, it includes sexual conduct outside the boundaries of marriage established in Scripture.
But notice something important.

Paul doesn't give believers a detailed chart specifying exactly how many seconds a kiss may last, which kinds of embraces are permitted, or the precise point at which every form of touching becomes sinful.
He gives them a moral direction.
Holiness.
Honor.
Self-control.
And a refusal to let sexual desire govern their behavior.
The Greek word ἁγιασμός — hagiasmos, translated “sanctification,” speaks of holiness or being set apart for God.
This is the heart of the matter.
God is not merely interested in whether you managed to avoid one particular physical act.
He cares about the person you are becoming while you pursue someone you love.
He cares about your integrity when nobody is watching.
He cares about whether your affection is governed by genuine love or increasingly controlled by appetite.
And He cares about the person sitting beside you.
Because that person is not simply your boyfriend.
Not simply your girlfriend.
Not simply your future spouse, even if you hope to marry.
That person bears the image of God.
Their body is not something you are entitled to explore simply because they love you.
Their conscience is not something you should pressure them to silence.
Their willingness to establish boundaries is not evidence that they love you less.
And their refusal to go further is not a rejection of your worth.
If your love requires someone to compromise their convictions to keep you happy, something about that love needs to change.
That sentence may hurt.
Especially if you've ever said, “But if you really loved me…”
Or if someone has said it to you.
Perhaps you didn't mean to manipulate them.
Perhaps you were afraid of losing them.
Perhaps you confused physical closeness with emotional security.
But love that honors Christ does not use fear, guilt, or emotional pressure to obtain intimacy.
First Corinthians 13:5 says that love “seeketh not her own.”
In context, Paul is describing love that is not selfishly demanding.
That principle has enormous implications for Christian relationships.
Love doesn't ask, “How far can I persuade you to go?”
Love asks, “How can I protect your dignity, honor your convictions, and help us both remain faithful to Christ?”
And no, that doesn't mean every kiss is sinful.
Let's be careful here.
The Bible does not explicitly prohibit every romantic kiss before marriage.
Anyone who claims Scripture provides an exact universal rule about the duration or intensity of every kiss is saying more than the text itself directly states.
But Scripture does command sexual purity, warns against lust, and calls believers to exercise wisdom and self-control.
That means the question cannot be settled by pretending every affectionate gesture is identical.
A brief expression of affection and a prolonged encounter intentionally designed to produce intense sexual arousal are not necessarily the same in purpose or effect.
Context matters.
Intent matters.
The effect on both people matters.
And the direction in which the relationship is moving matters.
Jesus said in Matthew 5:28:
“But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.”
The Greek expression πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν — pros to epithymēsai autēn concerns looking at a woman with lustful intent.
Jesus is exposing the moral significance of the heart, not declaring that every involuntary experience of attraction is equivalent to adultery.
Attraction is not automatically lust.
Recognizing someone's beauty is not automatically lust.
Experiencing sexual desire is not automatically a deliberate act of sin.
But choosing to cultivate lustful thoughts, reducing another person to an object for gratification, and deliberately pursuing sexual excitement outside marriage raises serious spiritual concerns.
That distinction matters.
Because some believers have been taught to feel guilty merely for having a body.
Others have been taught that anything short of intercourse is morally harmless.
Neither extreme adequately represents the biblical picture.
The Christian life is not about despising desire.
It's about bringing desire under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And that brings us to a passage many people have heard but few have considered deeply.
Second Timothy 2:22 says:
“Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace, with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart.”
The Greek verb φεῦγε — pheuge means “flee.”
Run away.
Escape.
Don't remain in the situation simply to prove how strong you are.
And notice that Paul doesn't merely tell Timothy what to flee.
He tells him what to pursue.
Righteousness.
Faith.
Love.
Peace.
In other words, Christian purity isn't supposed to become an obsession with avoiding mistakes while neglecting a vibrant relationship with God.
It is meant to be part of a life actively pursuing Christ.
Now picture two people who know that whenever they're alone late at night, their physical boundaries tend to collapse.
They've apologized.
They've prayed.
They've promised to do better.
But the next weekend, they return to the same environment, repeat the same behavior, and experience the same guilt.
At some point, they need more than another emotional promise.
They need wisdom expressed through actual change.
Perhaps that means spending less time alone in private bedrooms.
Perhaps it means avoiding overnight stays together.
Perhaps it means deciding not to engage in prolonged physical intimacy that repeatedly leads to sexual compromise.
Perhaps it means having an honest conversation with a trusted, mature Christian mentor.
Not because every couple must follow identical rules.
But because genuine repentance includes a willingness to change the circumstances that repeatedly facilitate sin.
And please hear this.
Boundaries are not evidence that love is weak. Sometimes they are evidence that love is finally becoming mature.
You don't need to test the edge of a cliff to prove that you trust God.
You don't need to discover exactly how close you can stand to temptation before falling.
You don't need to make obedience as difficult as possible.
Proverbs 4:23 says:
“Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.”
In Hebrew, the opening expression is מִכָּל־מִשְׁמָר נְצֹר לִבֶּךָ — mikol-mishmar netsor libbekha.
The sense is to guard your heart with exceptional vigilance.
In Proverbs, the heart is not merely the seat of romantic feelings. It encompasses the inner life—thoughts, desires, intentions, and decisions.
So guarding your heart is not simply refusing to develop feelings for someone.
It is learning to steward your entire inner life before God.
It means asking yourself questions you might prefer to avoid.
Am I pursuing this person because I genuinely want to love and serve them?
Or because physical intimacy makes me feel wanted?
Am I respecting their convictions?
Or trying to find a way around them?
Are we growing in honesty, patience, prayer, and responsibility?
Or are we becoming increasingly dependent on physical affection to hold the relationship together?
And perhaps the most difficult question of all:
If physical intimacy were temporarily removed from this relationship, would the love between us still have something substantial to stand on?
Don't rush past that.
Because some relationships feel extraordinarily deep when two people are physically close, yet become painfully fragile when they must communicate honestly, resolve conflict, or wait.
Physical affection can express genuine love.
But it cannot substitute for character.
It cannot create trust where honesty is absent.
It cannot produce faithfulness where self-control is missing.
And it cannot transform a relationship that is fundamentally unhealthy into a godly marriage.
Marriage itself is not a magical cure for selfishness or lust.
A wedding ceremony does not automatically teach someone how to respect boundaries, handle disappointment, or love sacrificially.
Those qualities must be cultivated through repentance, spiritual maturity, and grace.
And this is why the question “How far is too far?” deserves a more thoughtful answer than simply “Don't have sex.”
Biblically, sexual intercourse belongs within marriage.
Sexual acts that deliberately imitate or pursue the sexual intimacy reserved for marriage should not be treated as harmless loopholes merely because intercourse has not occurred.
At the same time, Scripture does not provide an exhaustive list classifying every possible gesture of premarital affection.
Christians should be honest about that distinction.
We must not invent divine commandments where God has not spoken explicitly.
But neither should we use biblical silence about particular gestures as permission to ignore the broader commands concerning holiness, lust, honor, and self-control.
Romans 13:14 says:
“But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof.”
That final instruction is remarkably practical.
Don't deliberately arrange your life around opportunities to indulge sinful desire.
If you already know that a particular activity consistently leads you toward sexual compromise, don't keep calling it harmless simply because it begins innocently.
If you know that lying together in bed makes it almost impossible to maintain your convictions, reconsider that practice.
If you know that certain forms of touching are intentionally sexual and repeatedly lead you beyond the boundaries you believe honor Christ, stop pretending the problem is merely a lack of willpower.
Change the pattern.
And if one person wants to stop, the other must respect that immediately.
Consent matters.
Personal boundaries matter.
No relationship status, engagement, previous sexual history, or promise of marriage gives anyone the right to another person's body.
Someone who genuinely loves you should never make you afraid to say no.
But now we need to talk about the person who has been reading this with a heavy heart.
The person who has already crossed the boundaries we've been discussing.
The person who once promised God they would wait.
And didn't.
Perhaps it happened gradually.
One compromise became another.
You told yourself it would be the last time.
Then it happened again.
Perhaps you were genuinely in love.
Perhaps you were lonely.
Perhaps you wanted to feel accepted.
Perhaps you knew what Scripture taught, but in that moment, your desire was louder than your conviction.
And now you wonder whether God sees you differently.
Whether your future marriage has been ruined.
Whether you're still worthy of love.
Whether you've lost something that can never be restored.
I want to speak to you with both tenderness and truth.
Sin is serious.
Scripture does not ask us to rename disobedience as freedom simply because repentance feels uncomfortable.
But Scripture also does not teach that a person's worth is destroyed by sexual sin.
Your value as a human being was never based on an untouched sexual history.
You bear God's image.
And the Gospel announces forgiveness and transformation through Jesus Christ to sinners who turn to Him in faith.
Listen to 1 Corinthians 6:9–11.
Paul names various sins, including sexual immorality, and then tells believers:
“And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.”
Read those words again.
“And such were some of you.”
Not because their past never happened.
Not because their actions were inconsequential.
But because their past was no longer the final word about who they were in Christ.
The Greek expression ἀπελούσασθε — apelousasthe, translated “ye are washed,” points to cleansing.
Paul connects this cleansing with sanctification and justification in the name of Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
The Gospel does not merely tell guilty people to try harder.
It announces what God has done through Christ to reconcile sinners to Himself.
And it calls those who belong to Him to live differently.
That's why repentance matters.
The Greek word μετάνοια — metanoia means repentance, involving a change of mind and direction.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling bad because you got caught.
More than crying after crossing a boundary.
More than promising to change while deliberately preserving the same pattern.
It is turning away from sin and toward God.
And sometimes repentance begins with a painfully honest confession:
“Lord, I wanted what I wanted more than I wanted to obey You.”
No excuses.
No pretending.
No blaming the other person for choices that were your own.
Just truth.
And the astonishing thing about the Gospel is that God does not require you to hide your sin until you've made yourself worthy of approaching Him.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Notice what the verse does not say.
It does not say God forgives only those who have never struggled sexually.
It does not say forgiveness is available only to people whose failures are socially acceptable.
It does not say your past becomes too complicated for Christ to redeem.
It calls us to confess.
And it points us to God's faithfulness.
But perhaps you're asking a different question.
“What if I've already had sex before marriage? Can I still have a godly marriage?”
Yes.
Your past does not automatically disqualify you from a faithful, Christ-centered marriage.
But that does not mean your past should be ignored.
Healing may require honest conversations.
Trust may need rebuilding.
Consequences may need to be addressed.
Some relationships may need serious reconsideration.
And if there has been coercion, exploitation, or abuse, the responsibility belongs to the person who committed the harm. Experiencing abuse is not a moral failure by the person who suffered it.
Godly restoration never requires someone to remain in an unsafe relationship.
Grace is not denial.
Grace gives us the courage to face the truth without believing that the truth makes redemption impossible.
And here is something else.
You do not have to marry someone simply because you've been sexually intimate with them.
Marriage is a covenant, not a punishment for past decisions.
Nor does repentance require you to return to a relationship that is harmful or manipulative.
The right response to sexual sin is not desperation.
It is surrender to Christ, wise counsel, and a renewed commitment to walk in truth.
Remember the woman brought before Jesus in John 8?

The account, traditionally known as the woman caught in adultery, has a well-known textual-history question: John 7:53–8:11 is absent from some of the earliest Greek manuscripts and appears in different locations in parts of the manuscript tradition. It should therefore not be treated as though its textual status is undisputed.
Nevertheless, the account as traditionally received vividly illustrates a distinction consistent with the wider New Testament witness: mercy does not require calling sin righteous.
Jesus tells the woman:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” (John 8:11, KJV)
Mercy.
And a call to change.
Not condemnation as entertainment.
Not permission to continue in sin.
And that balance is essential.
Because some people use purity teachings to crush wounded believers.
Others use grace as an excuse to dismiss holiness.
But Jesus cannot be faithfully reduced to either extreme.
The Christ who forgives sinners also calls them to follow Him.
The Christ who welcomes the repentant also transforms their lives.
The Christ who died for our sins did not die to make those sins irrelevant.
He died to save us.
And that brings us to a beautiful truth about marriage itself.
Ephesians 5:25 says:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
Think about the standard Paul establishes.
Christ's self-giving love.
Not entitlement.
Not manipulation.
Not consuming another person to satisfy yourself.
Sacrificial love.
Marriage is meant to reflect something of that covenantal faithfulness.
And while Paul's immediate instruction concerns husbands and wives, the moral character of Christlike love matters long before a wedding day.
If you hope to marry someone, ask yourself:
Am I learning to love this person in a way that reflects Jesus?
Can I be patient when desire is strong?
Can I honor a boundary without resentment?
Can I say, “I love you enough to wait,” and actually mean it?
Can I acknowledge when I've sinned instead of justifying myself?
Can we talk about difficult subjects without threatening, manipulating, or shaming one another?
Can we seek God's wisdom even when obedience costs us something we deeply want?
Because one of the most beautiful things you can offer someone you love is not merely physical restraint.
It is trustworthy character.
A heart that tells the truth.
A conscience that remains tender toward God.
A willingness to apologize.
A commitment to protect rather than exploit.
A love that doesn't disappear when gratification is delayed.
And for those who are engaged, hear this too.
Engagement is meaningful.
It expresses an intention to marry.
But it is not marriage itself.
The promise of a future covenant does not mean the covenant has already been entered.
You can celebrate your approaching wedding without treating your future spouse as though marriage has already begun.
Waiting may be difficult.
Sometimes deeply difficult.
But difficulty does not make obedience meaningless.
And if you are struggling, you don't have to pretend that the struggle isn't real.
Christian discipleship is not a competition to appear untouched by temptation.
It is a lifelong dependence on the grace and power of God.
Galatians 5:22–23 describes the fruit of the Spirit, including temperance, or self-control.
The Greek word ἐγκράτεια — enkrateia refers to self-mastery or self-control.
Notice that self-control is described as fruit of the Spirit.
This is not merely about human stubbornness.
It's about a life being reshaped by God's Spirit.
That doesn't eliminate the need for practical boundaries.
It gives those boundaries a deeper purpose.
You're not simply saying no to something.
You're learning to say yes to a greater allegiance.
Yes to Christ.
Yes to holiness.
Yes to honoring another person's dignity.
Yes to the possibility of entering marriage without deliberately cultivating patterns of sexual compromise.
And yes to trusting God even when His way requires patience.
Maybe you're reading this beside someone you love.
Maybe you've both been arguing about where the line should be.
Maybe one of you has felt pressured.
Maybe both of you have been quietly troubled by what has been happening.
Tonight, instead of having another conversation about how close you can get to the boundary, consider having a different conversation.
Ask each other whether your relationship is making it easier or harder to follow Jesus.
Ask whether your physical intimacy is expressing love responsibly or becoming something you struggle to govern.
Ask whether you've been respecting each other's convictions.
Ask whether there are situations you need to stop placing yourselves in.
And if necessary, pray together.
Not a dramatic prayer meant to erase the consequences of your choices.
An honest one.

“Lord Jesus, we love each other, but we have not always loved You faithfully in this relationship. Forgive us where we have sinned. Teach us to honor You with our bodies, our choices, and the way we treat one another. Give us courage to change what needs to change. Let our love become more patient, more truthful, and more like Yours. Amen.”
And if you're single, this message is for you too.
You don't need to wait until you're dating someone to develop convictions about sexual integrity.
You can begin now.
Not by living in fear of every future temptation.
But by learning what Scripture teaches, understanding your own vulnerabilities, building healthy friendships, and pursuing spiritual maturity.
You are not incomplete because you are unmarried.
You are not less valuable because you are waiting.
And you are not more valuable than someone else because your sexual history is different.
Your identity is not ultimately found in your relationship status or your past.
For those who belong to Christ, identity is rooted in Him.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
This does not mean every consequence of the past vanishes overnight.
It means union with Christ brings a fundamentally new reality.
A new allegiance.
A new hope.
A new direction.
A life no longer defined solely by what came before.
And that is why our message at Gospel Warrior will never simply be “Stay pure or you're ruined.”
No.
Our message is that Jesus Christ is holy, His commands are good, sin is serious, and His grace is sufficient to forgive and transform those who turn to Him.
From hiding to confession.
From compromise to repentance.
From shame to a new beginning.
Not because sin was insignificant.
But because the Savior is greater.
And perhaps that is the answer you've needed all along.
How far is too far?

Too far is not a single distance that can be measured with a ruler. Scripture establishes the moral boundary of sexual intimacy within marriage and calls us to avoid lust and sexual immorality. Wisdom then asks us to establish practical boundaries that genuinely help us obey those commands.
Don't turn the absence of an explicit rule about every gesture into an excuse to abandon discernment.
Don't treat personal boundaries as though they are universal biblical commandments.
Don't mistake temptation for automatic guilt.
Don't mistake sexual desire for something inherently shameful.
And don't confuse forgiveness with permission to keep deliberately returning to sin.
Instead, bring the entire relationship under the lordship of Jesus.
Your intentions.
Your conversations.
Your physical affection.
Your private habits.
Your hopes for marriage.
Your willingness to wait.
Your willingness to repent.
All of it.
Because the greatest question is not simply whether you can approach marriage without crossing a particular physical line.
It's whether you're becoming someone who can love another person faithfully, sacrificially, and truthfully.
And whether, married or unmarried, your life belongs to Christ.
Now I want to speak directly to the person who almost stopped reading because this message touched something painful.
Maybe nobody knows what you've been struggling with.
Maybe your relationship looks spiritually healthy from the outside, but privately you've been making compromises you never expected to make.
Maybe you feel exhausted by repeated failure.
Maybe you're afraid to tell someone because you don't want to be judged.
You do not have to publish your private history to prove that you're repentant.
You do not have to disclose intimate details to strangers.
But you can stop hiding from God.
You can seek wise, confidential pastoral counsel.
You can make changes today.
And you can remember that the invitation of Christ is not reserved for people who have never failed.
Matthew 11:28 says:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
Come to Him.
Not because you're already perfect.
But because you need Him.
Not because your struggle is small.
But because His mercy is real.
Not because you can save yourself through enough self-discipline.
But because salvation is by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, and the life of faith bears fruit in obedience.
You can simply write “Lord, teach me to honor You.”
And if you have a testimony or a question about Christian dating and boundaries, you're welcome to share what you're comfortable sharing. You never need to reveal intimate personal details.
Your honesty may encourage someone who thought they were the only one fighting this battle.
Not because reading it once will solve every struggle.
But because there may come a night when you need to remember why you established a boundary in the first place.
You may never know who quietly reads it and finds the courage to have an honest conversation, seek forgiveness, or choose a wiser path.
We want this to be a place where people can encounter Scripture, wrestle honestly with difficult questions, hear the Gospel of Jesus Christ, and grow in spiritual maturity.
And if this ministry has helped you grow, I want to invite you to consider something deeper.
And not because a monthly payment can purchase forgiveness, spiritual favor, or salvation.
The grace of God is not for sale.
But Scripture does teach that believers may voluntarily support faithful Gospel ministry.
Galatians 6:6 encourages those who receive instruction in the Word to share good things with those who teach.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
And that is the spirit in which we invite you.
Think of the person who has never opened a Bible but might read a Gospel Warrior article.
The young believer who feels trapped in a cycle of compromise.
The husband or wife quietly seeking restoration.
The teenager searching for answers about relationships.
The wounded Christian who needs to hear that repentance and forgiveness are still possible through Jesus Christ.
These items can serve as reminders of biblical truth, tools for reflection, or meaningful gifts for others.
It is the opportunity to participate voluntarily in sustaining a ministry that seeks to point people to Jesus.
You can still pray for the ministry.
You can still read, learn, and grow.
You can still help put biblical truth in front of someone who may desperately need it.
Financial support matters for sustaining ministry, but your worth before God is not measured by what you give.
And above all, the purpose of everything we do must remain Jesus Christ.
Not our platform.
Not our popularity.
Jesus.
The One who calls us out of darkness.
The One who tells us the truth about sin.
The One who receives those who repent and believe.
The One whose death and resurrection are the foundation of our hope.
The One who can transform a life that seemed hopelessly tangled in shame.
So before you leave, return with me to that quiet moment where this article began.
Two people sitting close together.
A relationship filled with feelings.
A conscience asking questions.
A choice waiting to be made.
Maybe the most loving thing they can do tonight is stop.
Maybe it's having an uncomfortable conversation.
Maybe it's admitting that their boundaries have not been working.
Maybe it's asking for forgiveness.
Maybe it's choosing to walk away from a relationship that has become coercive or destructive.
Maybe it's deciding that Jesus deserves more than the leftovers of their obedience.
And maybe, for the first time, they will understand that waiting isn't simply about what they refuse to do with their bodies.
It's about Whom they are learning to trust with their lives.
One day, you may stand before someone and promise lifelong faithfulness.
Or perhaps your calling will take a different path.
Either way, the most important relationship you will ever have is not with a future husband or wife.
It is with the Lord Jesus Christ.
Don't sacrifice your relationship with Him to preserve a moment of pleasure.
And if you already have fallen, don't allow shame to convince you that you can never rise again.
Come to Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Receive His grace through faith.
And walk forward in the new life He gives.
Because your story does not have to end where your compromise began.
The hands that were pierced for your redemption are still the hands calling you out of hiding and into the light.
